## Introduction

Bibliometric software often assumes that you can export records from a
subscription database such as Scopus or Web of Science. Many students,
institutional researchers, and small teams cannot. What they do have is a
reference-manager library (RefWorks, or anything that exports RIS), a set of
Google Scholar searches, or a BibTeX file collected by hand.

`citelens` is a workaround for that situation. It takes the records you *can*
get and turns them into analysis-ready data frames, then runs text analytics on
the abstracts. It does four things:

1. **Converts** RefWorks and RIS exports, and saved Google Scholar results
   pages, to BibTeX.
2. **Reads** BibTeX into a data frame or an Excel workbook.
3. **Fills in** missing abstracts by looking them up in
   [OpenAlex](https://openalex.org), a free scholarly index.
4. **Analyzes** abstracts: topic modeling (latent Dirichlet allocation),
   cosine document similarity with duplicate finding, and trends over time.

The parsing and the computationally heavy steps are written in C++ through
`Rcpp`, so the package stays fast on large libraries.

`citelens` does not try to replace general-purpose tools. If you can already
export from a major database, or you want a full science-mapping toolkit
(co-citation networks, collaboration maps, and so on), packages such as
`bibliometrix` and `openalexR` are built for that. `citelens` is for the earlier
steps of getting a messy library into shape, and for abstract-level text
analysis that does not need a paid database.

## Installation

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("citelens")
```

The C++ code is compiled when you install, so you need a C++ compiler: the
Xcode command line tools on macOS, Rtools on Windows, or `build-essential` (or
your distribution's equivalent) on Linux.

```{r load}
library(citelens)
```

## Sample data

The package ships with small sample files so that every example below can be
run as is.

```{r sample-files}
list.files(system.file("extdata", package = "citelens"))
```

* `sample_refworks.ris` and `sample_refworks.txt`: a few references in RIS and
  RefWorks Tagged Format.
* `sample.bib`: the same references as BibTeX.
* `sample_abstracts.bib`: 30 *synthetic* abstracts for trying the text
  analytics. The text is made up, so the results are for illustration only.

## Converting a RefWorks or RIS export

`convert_refworks()` reads a RefWorks export and returns BibTeX entries. It
accepts both **RefWorks Tagged Format** (lines such as `RT`, `A1`, `T1`) and
**RIS** (lines such as `TY  -`, `AU  -`), and detects which one you supplied.

```{r convert}
ris <- system.file("extdata", "sample_refworks.ris", package = "citelens")
entries <- convert_refworks(ris)
cat(entries[1])
```

Citation keys are built from the first author, the year, and the first
meaningful word of the title (for example `tinto2006research`). A letter is
added when two keys would otherwise collide. Reference types are mapped to
BibTeX types (journal article to `article`, book chapter to `incollection`,
thesis to `phdthesis`, and so on); anything unrecognized becomes `misc`.

To write a `.bib` file, give `convert_refworks()` an output path:

```{r convert-file}
bib_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".bib")
convert_refworks(ris, bib_file)
file.exists(bib_file)
```

### From RefWorks straight to Excel

If a spreadsheet is what you need, `refworks_to_xlsx()` does the whole job in
one step. It can also keep the BibTeX copy.

```{r refworks-xlsx}
xlsx_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".xlsx")
refs <- refworks_to_xlsx(ris, xlsx_file, bib = tempfile(fileext = ".bib"))
file.exists(xlsx_file)
```

The data frame is returned invisibly, so you can keep working with it in R.

## Reading BibTeX into a data frame

`bib_to_df()` reads any BibTeX file, whether it came from `convert_refworks()`,
Google Scholar's **Cite > BibTeX** option, or another tool.

```{r bib-to-df}
refs <- bib_to_df(system.file("extdata", "sample.bib", package = "citelens"))
refs[, c("bibtype", "bibkey", "year", "title")]
```

The result has one row per entry. `bibtype` and `bibkey` come first, followed by
one column for every BibTeX field found in the file. Fields an entry does not
have are `NA`, and every column is character, so convert `year` with
`as.integer()` if you need to do arithmetic on it.

By default the values are cleaned: grouping braces are removed (`{{Title}}`
becomes `Title`), escapes such as `\&` are undone, and extra whitespace is
collapsed. Use `clean = FALSE` for the raw values. Files saved with Windows-1252
curly quotes or hidden control characters are repaired as they are read, so the
Excel output opens cleanly.

You can also save a workbook while reading:

```{r bib-to-xlsx, eval = FALSE}
refs <- bib_to_df("references.bib", xlsx = "references.xlsx")
```

## Google Scholar results

Google Scholar has no public API and blocks automated requests, so `citelens`
never contacts it. Instead, you save a results page from your browser
(**File > Save Page As**, then "Webpage, HTML Only") and let the package read the
saved file.

```{r scholar, eval = FALSE}
# one page
res <- scholar_parse_html("~/Downloads/scholar_page1.html")

# a whole folder: every .html file is read and combined
res <- scholar_parse_html("~/Documents/scholar_pages")

# include subfolders
res <- scholar_parse_html("~/Documents/scholar_pages", recursive = TRUE)

# straight to BibTeX; repeated results are removed
scholar_html_to_bib("~/Documents/scholar_pages", "scholar.bib")
```

Files in the folder that are not Scholar results pages are skipped with a
warning that names them. The `source_file` column shows which file each result
came from.

A results list is a summary, not a full record. It gives title, authors, venue,
year, publisher, and link, but it shortens long author lists and venue names
with "...", and it has no volume, pages, DOI, or abstract. Shortened entries are
flagged (a `note` field in the BibTeX; `authors_truncated` and `venue_truncated`
columns in the data frame) so you can find them. When you need complete records,
use Scholar's **Cite > BibTeX**, or its **RefWorks / RefMan** exports, which
`bib_to_df()` and `convert_refworks()` read directly.

## Looking up missing abstracts in OpenAlex

Text analytics need abstracts, and Scholar's results list has none.
`fetch_abstracts()` looks them up in OpenAlex, by DOI when you have one and by
title otherwise.

OpenAlex requires a free API key:

1. Create a free account at <https://openalex.org>.
2. Copy your key from <https://openalex.org/settings/api>.
3. Save it once in R. It is picked up automatically afterward.

```{r api-key, eval = FALSE}
Sys.setenv(OPENALEX_API_KEY = "your-key")   # this session only
# To keep it permanently, add OPENALEX_API_KEY=your-key to your .Renviron file.
```

The examples below send requests over the internet, so they are not run when
this vignette is built.

```{r fetch, eval = FALSE}
res <- scholar_parse_html("~/Downloads/scholar_page1.html")
res <- fetch_abstracts(res)          # or fetch_abstracts(res, api_key = "your-key")

# the same, but straight to BibTeX with abstracts included
scholar_html_to_bib("scholar_page1.html", "scholar.bib", abstracts = TRUE)
```

`fetch_abstracts()` also works on a `bib_to_df()` table that has DOIs.

**What is sent.** Each title (or DOI) and your key are sent to OpenAlex, and
nothing else.

**Being careful about matches.** A title match is accepted only when the titles
are very close *and* the publication years agree to within a year. Otherwise the
abstract stays `NA`, because a missing abstract is better than the wrong one.
Many works in OpenAlex have no abstract on file, so expect gaps.

**Diagnosing gaps.** The `abstract_status` column says what happened to each
reference:

```{r status, eval = FALSE}
table(res$abstract_status)

# titles that did not match, with the closest candidate found
res[res$abstract_status == "title not matched",
    c("title", "closest_title", "closest_score")]

# if the closest titles are the right papers, accept looser matches
res <- fetch_abstracts(res, min_match = 0.75)

# "year differs": the title matched but the years are far apart
# (re-editions, online-first dates)
res[res$abstract_status == "year differs", c("title", "year", "closest_year")]
res <- fetch_abstracts(res, max_year_diff = 10)
```

The statuses are `found`, `no abstract on file`, `title not matched`,
`year differs`, `no results`, and `lookup failed`. Only the still-missing
references are retried when you run the function again on its own result. The
columns `abstract_match` and `abstract_source` help you spot-check what was
found.

**Usage limits.** A free key currently allows a daily allowance of credits, and
a title lookup costs more than a DOI lookup, so a few thousand references fit in
a day. If the allowance runs out, the function stops and keeps what it found.
Run it again later on the same object and it picks up where it left off.

## Topic modeling

The text analytics all work on a data frame with an `abstract` column, such as
the output of `bib_to_df()`. If your column has a different name, pass it with
`text = "..."`.

```{r refs-abstracts}
refs <- bib_to_df(system.file("extdata", "sample_abstracts.bib",
                              package = "citelens"))
nrow(refs)
```

`topic_model()` fits a latent Dirichlet allocation model to the abstracts. Set a
`seed` so the result is reproducible.

```{r topic-model}
m <- topic_model(refs, k = 3, seed = 1)
m
```

Printing the model gives each topic's prevalence, a coherence score, and its top
words. The helpers return the same information as data frames:

```{r topic-helpers}
topic_terms(m, n = 5)      # top words per topic
topic_summary(m)           # one row per topic
```

`topic_documents()` adds each abstract's dominant topic to your table, along
with the probability of that topic and the full topic mixture:

```{r topic-documents}
refs2 <- topic_documents(m, refs)
head(refs2[, c("title", "dominant_topic", "dominant_prob")])
```

Two charts summarize a model:

```{r topic-plots}
plot_topic_terms(m)
plot_topic_prevalence(m)
```

### Choosing the number of topics

There is no single correct `k`. `topic_k_search()` fits models for a range of
values so you can compare them, and `plot()` draws the comparison.

```{r k-search}
ks <- topic_k_search(refs, k = 2:5, seed = 1)
plot(ks)
```

Treat this as a guide and read the topics themselves. A `k` whose topics you can
name and defend is usually better than one that wins on a statistic.

### Tips

* Topic models work best with dozens of abstracts or more. The functions warn
  when you supply very few.
* Words that carry no meaning in your field can be dropped with
  `stopwords = c("student", "college")`. The built-in list is available from
  `citelens_stopwords()`.
* `max_doc_prop = 0.5` drops words found in more than half the abstracts.
* Before modeling, words are lower-cased, punctuation and numbers are removed,
  common English words and abstract boilerplate ("study", "results", and so on)
  are dropped, and simple plurals are merged ("student" and "students" count as
  one).

## Document similarity

`doc_similarity()` compares every pair of abstracts using cosine similarity of
TF-IDF word weights.

```{r similarity}
s <- doc_similarity(refs)
s
```

Find the closest matches to one paper, or look for likely duplicate entries:

```{r similar-to}
similar_to(s, "syn01", n = 3, data = refs)
find_duplicates(s, cutoff = 0.8, data = refs)
```

`plot_similarity()` draws a heatmap with similar abstracts grouped together:

```{r similarity-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6}
plot_similarity(s)
```

To work with the numbers, `similarity_to_df()` returns them as a data frame, in
either a matrix layout (one row and column per reference) or a pairs layout (one
row per pair, most similar first):

```{r similarity-df}
head(similarity_to_df(s, "pairs", data = refs), 5)
```

Add `xlsx = "similarity.xlsx"` to also save an Excel workbook with both
layouts, and `cutoff = 0.5` to keep only pairs at or above that similarity.

Similarity reflects shared vocabulary, not shared meaning. Two abstracts on
different subjects can look alike if they use the same technical language, so
use `stopwords =` to remove words common to your whole collection.

## Trends over time

The trend functions need a `year` column. `word_trends()` shows the share of
abstracts mentioning each word, by year or by group of years:

```{r word-trends}
w <- word_trends(refs, words = c("retention", "persistence", "dropout"),
                 bin = 3)
w
plot_word_trends(w)
```

`bin` groups years; `bin = 3` uses three-year periods. If you leave `words` as
`NULL`, the most common words are used.

`topic_trends()` does the same for topics, using a fitted model:

```{r topic-trends}
tt <- topic_trends(m, refs, bin = 3)
plot_topic_trends(tt)
```

Check `n_period`, the number of abstracts in each period. Periods with only a
few abstracts give jumpy shares, so avoid reading much into them.

## Using the results with other tools

Because `citelens` produces ordinary BibTeX files, data frames, and Excel
workbooks, you can hand its output to other tools.

* The `.bib` file opens in any reference manager that reads BibTeX.
* The data frames work with the usual R tools (`dplyr`, `ggplot2`, and others).
* The Excel files can be opened in Excel or imported by other software.

Packages that expect records in a specific database layout, such as the field
names used by Scopus or Web of Science, may need extra renaming of columns
before they accept the data. Check the documentation of the tool you plan to
use.

## Good to know

* The text analytics skip references with no abstract and tell you how many were
  skipped.
* All data frame columns are character, including `year`.
* Accent commands such as `{\'e}` are left as LaTeX when reading BibTeX.
* BibTeX features supported when reading include `@string` macros, month names,
  `#` concatenation, and `{...}`, `"..."`, and `(...)` delimiters. `@comment`
  and `@preamble` blocks are ignored.
* Topic modeling and similarity describe the *text* of abstracts. They are
  exploratory tools, not substitutes for reading the papers.

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```
